I have thought of another way to compare pattern size: total cell value.  The quadratic pattern I just posted is also the smallest known in total cell value.

For infinite linear growth, the smallest known is 5 (the 3x3 pattern with 3 cells).

Of course, we have arbitrarily selected one state to be "1" and the other to be "2", rendering this almost meaningless.  It has slightly more meaning for totalistic rules, or any rule in which the numerical value of the cell is used in the step function.

simsim314 wrote:Here is 5 cells quadratic...
I take it you've done some searching for 4-cell quadratic-growth patterns, without finding anything?  It looks like there's some hope for such a search, but it isn't trivial to decide which patterns will end up with quadratic growth.

For example, here's a 4-cell infinite-growth pattern that doesn't stop producing novel reactions until about 2.185 million ticks:

Code: Select all / Show in Viewerx = 30, y = 16, rule = Serizawa
B2$3.B2$B11$29.A!
Any of probably hundreds of similar slow-to-settle patterns might end up in a stable rake-building orbit; no way to tell for sure without running each one until the novelty works its way out.  Another 4-cell with good novelty potential early on is

Code: Select all / Show in Viewerx = 30, y = 28, rule = Serizawa
B2$3.B2$B23$29.A!
EDIT: Yikes!  Here's one with a series of false alarms early on, but then it starts doing really interesting quadratic-growth stuff around 3.5M ticks.  It's hard to run this one far enough to see if the expanding region will be able to escape from the box that it starts in:

Code: Select all / Show in Viewer#C 4-cell Serizawa quadratic-growth candidate --
#C moving the key cell by (2,1) appears to have the same effect
x = 32, y = 24, rule = Serizawa
B2$3.B2$B19$31.A!


By 3.74 million ticks the rake-making region seems to be strictly bounded -- as many rakes are being destroyed as created, so no long-term quadratic growth after all.  Of course it's quite possible that another quadratic-growth region will start up somewhere in this monster -- novelty clearly isn't exhausted yet -- but it may make sense to look for a simpler example of 4-cell quadratic growth...!

dvgrn wrote:... it may make sense to look for a simpler example of 4-cell quadratic growth.
Found one, with a slightly-revised search script -- originally I was only looking 16K ticks ahead, not nearly far enough to catch late novelty appearances.  Now I'm waiting to see if it looks quadratic at 2 million ticks.  Even that may not be enough in a few cases, but for the most part Hashlife is happily running away with the pattern by T=2M.

Code: Select all / Show in Viewerx = 35, y = 20, rule = Serizawa
B2$3.B2$B15$34.A!
Don't expect anything interesting to happen until 44K ticks, when the rake-making puffer appears more or less out of nowhere.  Unfortunately this is still not an entirely predictable quadratic growth rate, because of a secondary puffer that shows up at 77K and starts transforming the output of the first puffer in unpredictable ways.  The search for simplicity continues...

simsim314 wrote:Found it! Very clear 4 cell quadratic...
Ah, good -- congratulations!  Now I won't be distracted by this search any longer.

I looked at lots of false positives, mostly within 60 cells of the 3-cell.  The odds of interesting novelty seemed to go down significantly, about 40 cells from the 3-cell, and cells to the right seemed to give better results on average than cells to the left, so I hadn't tried running a search that far out yet.

The complex maybe-quadratic "novelty generators" that I posted above remind me of some of Bill Gosper's experiments in Conway's Life from a few years ago.  Different types of puffers and rakes have different large-scale signatures in a long-running pattern.  It might be possible to find a few new rakes or puffers in Serizawa by looking for unfamiliar fingerprints in these patterns, in the same way that you can recognize switch engines in a zoomed-out Life pattern.

Anyway we also should prove that quadratic is impossible with 3. Probably some kind of brute force.

EDIT

I was thinking of GOL quadratic search, and the problem is that linear growth is so much rear in life unlike in Serizawa where it's pretty common. This makes the quadratic patterns in Life even more rear, so the current 26 cells record can't be so simply beaten. The current search in Serizawa with minor optimization took me an hour or two, in GOL it would probably take weeks even months.

simsim314 wrote:Yes there is a lot of "quadratic mess". Here is an example of something which I couldn't even figure out if it quadratic or not, because it's so messy, and it's simply stuck golly before the growth rate is clear...
Wow, that's an impressive one.  By 1.5M ticks it seems to have decided to go quadratic in the first and third quadrants, anyway.

The second quadrant is prolific enough that it will also contribute significantly to the population count.  Probably the vertical bars will continue to appear irregularly, or they might settle into periodicity eventually... there's some fairly complicated recursive math happening there, with gliders from lower down bubbling up unpredictably to start new northward puffers.  Anyway, it's certainly not clear that even an approximate growth rate can be calculated without running this one a lot farther.

Not bad for a four-cell starting pattern!
